summary: Discusses how L2TP can use IPsec to provide tunnel authentication, privacy, integrity checking, and replay protection, covering both voluntary and compulsory tunneling.

eli5.summary: It puts a locked, sealed tube around a tunnel so no one can peek or fake it.

questions: how to secure l2tp with ipsec

subtitle: How to protect L2TP tunnels with IPsec ESP and IKE, including the filter rules when ports and addresses move.

tldr.problem: L2TP tunnels PPP over networks but defines no protection for the tunnel itself, so control and data packets can be snooped, modified, hijacked or used for denial of service.
tldr.mechanism: Implementations MUST use IPsec ESP for L2TP control and data packets, with transport mode required, and SHOULD use IKE for authentication and key management. The RFC also gives filtering rules so IPsec still works when L2TP floats its UDP ports or the responder's IP address.
tldr.outcome: L2TP gets per-packet authentication, integrity and replay protection that neither L2TP tunnel authentication nor PPP provides. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Required IPsec protocol
facts.value: ESP, transport mode MUST be supported

today: RFC 3193 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 2661 (L2TP) and the IPsec specifications it cites, such as RFC 2406 and RFC 2409.

sections.title: Why L2TP Needs IPsec
sections.content:
L2TP tunnels PPP traffic over a variety of networks (the RFC names IP, SONET and ATM). It inherits PPP authentication, the PPP Encryption Control Protocol (ECP) and the Compression Control Protocol (CCP), and it can mutually authenticate the tunnel endpoints. But it defines no tunnel protection mechanisms.

RFC 3193 proposes using the IPsec suite (the architecture, IKE, AH and ESP) to protect L2TP over IP networks. It does not try to standardize end-to-end security: when that is needed, additional mechanisms such as IPsec or TLS should be used inside the tunnel. The scope is limited to L2TP over IP. The RFC distinguishes voluntary tunneling, where the user creates the tunnel (or a gateway does, in the gateway-to-gateway case), from compulsory tunneling, where the NAS/LAC tunnels the client's PPP packets with no client choice. The initiator is whichever side sends the SCCRQ, and the responder is the side that answers with an SCCRP.
sections.eli5: L2TP builds a hidden pipe for messages, but the pipe itself has no lock. IPsec supplies the lock.

sections.title: Security Requirements and the ESP Choice
sections.content:
Both control and data packets are exposed. The RFC lists attacks such as snooping user identities, modifying packets, hijacking the tunnel or the PPP connection inside it, ending connections for denial of service, and disrupting PPP ECP or authentication negotiation to weaken protection.

The security protocol MUST give authentication, integrity and replay protection for control packets and SHOULD protect their confidentiality. For data packets it MUST give integrity and replay protection and MAY protect confidentiality. It MUST also offer scalable key management. L2TP tunnel authentication happens only at tunnel origination, PPP authenticates only the client to the LNS, and PPP encryption lacks authentication, integrity, replay protection and key management, so none of them meets these needs.

To meet them, compliant implementations MUST implement IPsec ESP for control and data packets. Transport mode MUST be supported and tunnel mode MAY be. All IPsec-mandated ciphersuites, including NULL encryption, MUST be supported, though the operator chooses which to use; NULL encryption suits traffic such as L2TP data where confidentiality is not needed. IPsec replay protection MUST be implemented, and IKE SHOULD be supported for authentication, SA negotiation and key management.

The RFC also prefers stateless compression and encryption over IP, because stateful methods magnify packet losses and L2TP does not require packet ordering.
sections.eli5: The rules say every packet must be checked for tampering and for being a repeat, and the lock must be the standard IPsec one.

sections.title: Interoperability Guidelines
sections.content:
When the L2TP tunnel is deleted by either peer, any phase 1 and phase 2 SAs left over from it SHOULD be deleted, and delete messages SHOULD be sent. When IKE receives such a delete, it should tell L2TP. Once a ZLB ack has been sent in response to a StopCCN, the tunnel state and its filters can safely be removed.

Adding L2TP and IPsec headers to a PPP frame can cause fragmentation, since the default PPP MRU is 1500 bytes. One mitigation is to give PPP the MTU of the tunnel's interface minus the extra header overhead, after the L2TP tunnel is set up and before LCP negotiation begins. If IPsec receives an ICMP path MTU message, it should store the value in the SA and notify L2TP.

For every packet arriving from a tunnel that requires security, L2TP MUST check that IPsec decrypted or authenticated it, and MUST verify that the IP addresses and UDP ports match the socket information used to set up the tunnel. The second check stops malicious peers from spoofing packets into other tunnels.
sections.eli5: Clean up locks when a tunnel closes, make packets small enough to fit with the extra wrapping, and always check that each packet really came through the lock.

sections.title: IPsec Filtering for Floating Ports and Addresses
sections.content:
IKE and IPsec usually need no integration with the application, but L2TP lets the UDP port float during negotiation. The responder may use a dynamically assigned source port, shown in the SCCRP. L2TP also lets the responder use a new IP address in the SCCRP, but implementations protected by IPsec SHOULD NOT do this. If the responder does pick a new address, it MUST send a StopCCN with Result Code 2 (General Error) and Error Code 7 (Try Another), with the ASCII encoded address as the only content of the error message. The initiator then MUST send a new SCCRQ to that address.

With pre-shared keys, a key must exist per peer. In Main Mode it must correspond to the peer's IP address, and in Aggressive Mode to a valid IPsec DOI ID type. The initiator MAY bind the original key to the new address. Pre-shared keys are hard to manage as endpoints grow, so certificates are preferred where possible.

In IKE phase 2 the Quick Mode IDs say which traffic is protected. The RFC solves the most general case (initiator picks a new port, responder picks a new address and port), which covers all eight combinations. The initial filters must exist before tunnel setup messages flow. L2TP should not retransmit the SCCRQ while the SA is still being set up, and if the SA cannot be set up, the packet MUST be dropped. The initiator MUST allow the responder to float its port and SHOULD allow a new IP address. In gateway-to-gateway and dial-out cases either side may start the tunnel, so both need an inbound filter accepting SCCRQs to port 1701.
sections.eli5: Normally the lock rules say 'protect messages on this road'. When L2TP may switch roads halfway, the rules have to be updated on the fly so the new road is locked too.

sections.title: IKE and PPP Authentication
sections.content:
PPP authenticates only at the start; it gives no per-packet authentication, integrity or replay protection. With IPsec, the keys derived from the authenticated IKE identity verify every packet. If the PPP identity is a user and the IKE identity is a machine, only the machine is checked per packet. Where only machine authentication is supported, any user on a multi-user machine will typically be able to send traffic down the tunnel. If IPsec supports user authentication, the client MUST make sure only that user's traffic is sent down the tunnel.

With X.509 certificates, the LNS is expected to send a Certificate Request Payload for a particular CA, and SHOULD be able to trust several CAs. Revocation checking MAY be enabled per CA. Machine or user certificates may be used. The RFC advises strictly controlled enrollment: a certificate that can be obtained with just a password has no more security value than the password.

Pre-shared keys in Main Mode are vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks in remote access, where dynamic IP addresses force a group key. Anyone with the group key can then masquerade as the LNS and attack legacy methods such as CHAP. Aggressive Mode avoids this but exposes the user identity. L2TP/IPsec implementations SHOULD NOT use a group pre-shared key for IKE authentication to the LNS, and pre-shared keys SHOULD be protected like the user's account password.
sections.eli5: Showing your ID once at the door is not the same as having it checked on every package. IPsec checks every package, but it may only know which computer sent it, not which person.

sections.title: IPsec and PPP Security Interactions
sections.content:
With IPsec protecting L2TP, both PPP and IPsec security services exist, and which are used depends on whether the tunnel is compulsory or voluntary. The RFC says these scenarios are non-normative.

In a compulsory tunnel the client sends PPP frames to the LAC and usually does not know about security between the LAC and the LNS, while the LNS can learn it by reading the properties of the SA. The client therefore usually wants end-to-end IPsec or PPP encryption of its own, and the LAC may negotiate ESP with null encryption with the LNS, so encryption is not duplicated and LAC scalability improves.

In a voluntary tunnel the client sends L2TP packets to the NAS, which routes them to the LNS. The client and the LNS then have symmetric knowledge of the security in place and can typically avoid PPP encryption and compression in favor of IPsec services. Duplicate encryption can still occur if the end-station is IPsec-capable, and avoiding it may require two SAs with the LNS. The RFC notes many IPsec implementations cannot support this without allowing L2TP packets on one tunnel from multiple UDP ports, which would need changes to the L2TP specification.
sections.eli5: Who knows about the lock depends on who set up the tunnel. If the user built it, everyone knows. If the dial-in company built it, the user does not know, so they bring their own lock.

sections.title: Example Filter Sets
sections.content:
Appendix A walks through filter sets for IPv4, noting that IPv6 would be similar. In the simplest case both sides use fixed addresses and ports, with the example addresses 1.1.1.1 for the initiator and 2.2.2.1 for the responder, and nothing changes during tunnel setup. The initiator still keeps an inbound filter for any source port, because it cannot know whether the responder will change its port.

The second example is a gateway-to-gateway tunnel with dynamic ports, where either side may initiate. The initiator uses port 5000 and the responder moves to port 6000. An extra phase 2 negotiation is needed to protect the SCCRP, and the responder's L2TP must inject an extra filter once it picks the new port. Once the tunnel is established, the original phase 2 may be deleted, which lets the Inbound-2 and Outbound-2 filters be removed.
sections.eli5: The examples show the exact lock lists for a simple case and a harder case where one side changes its door number midway.

messages.label: SCCRQ
messages.note: Protected by IKE phase 1 and phase 2; initial address.

messages.label: StopCCN
messages.note: Carries the new IP address in the error message.

messages.label: SCCRQ
messages.note: Sent to the new address after a new IKE phase 1 and phase 2.

messages.label: SCCRP
messages.note: Responder chooses a new port; a new IKE phase 2 protects it.

items.desc: The error message MUST then hold the ASCII encoded address to use.
